report:
# Does Offering HIV Self-Testing Increase HIV Testing Uptake?

**Yes — the evidence strongly supports this.** Multiple systematic reviews and meta-analyses of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) consistently show that offering HIV self-testing (HIVST) significantly increases the proportion of people who test for HIV, compared to standard testing services alone.

## Key Evidence

A systematic review and meta-analysis published in eClinicalMedicine (2021), based on 13 RCTs with moderate-certainty evidence, found that HIVST **more than doubled** testing uptake overall (RR: 2.09; 95% CI: 1.69–2.58; p < 0.0001) ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2589537021002716)).

A separate meta-analysis focusing on men who have sex with men (MSM) and transgender people found HIVST increased testing uptake by 1.45 times (RR = 1.45; 95% CI: 1.20–1.75), and also increased testing *frequency* — a meta-analysis of three RCTs found HIVST increased the mean number of HIV tests by 2.56 over follow-up, without negative effects on linkage to care, STI testing, condom use, or social harm ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7713313/)).

This body of evidence directly informed global policy: the World Health Organization has recommended HIVST since 2016 as "a safe, accurate and effective way to reach people who may not test otherwise, including people from key populations, men and young people" ([who.int](https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/WHO-CDS-HIV-19.36)).

A subsequent PMC review reinforces that "numerous randomized controlled trials found that offering HIVST increases HIV testing rates," though it notes most trials used free oral self-tests, which may affect generalizability to paid or blood-based tests ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8915955/)).

## Conclusion

The RCT evidence is consistent and robust across multiple independent meta-analyses: offering HIVST causally increases both the uptake and frequency of HIV testing, particularly among key populations like MSM, without apparent harms — supporting the "yes" answer with high confidence.
